root.note: A compound of vindr ‘wind’ and auga ‘eye’. Both parts are ordinary Germanic words: wind is English too, and auga is a cousin of eye.

stages.meaning: wind-eye: an opening in a roof or wall
an opening in a wall with glass in it

history: Window came to English with the Vikings. In Old Norse, the language of the Scandinavian settlers in England, vindauga meant ‘wind-eye’: a hole in the roof or wall where smoke and wind went out and light came in. Early windows had no glass. Before the Norse word arrived, Old English used ēagþyrel, an ‘eye-hole’. In Middle English people could also say fenester, from Latin fenestra, which is still the word in French (fenêtre) and German (Fenster). But the Norse word won. Window is one of many everyday English words from Old Norse, together with sky, egg, knife and even they.
historyEinfach: Window is a Viking word. The Vikings came from the north, from Scandinavia. In their language, vindauga meant ‘wind-eye’. It was a hole in the wall. Wind came in, and light came in. There was no glass. The old English word was ‘eye-hole’. Later English took the Viking word, and it became window.

elsewhere.text: Spanish ventana is not related to window, but it uses the same picture: it comes from Latin ventus, ‘wind’. A window was the place where the wind came in.
Russian окно is built from the Slavic word for eye, око. So Russian sees the eye, Spanish sees the wind, and English window has both: wind and eye.
German Fenster comes from Latin fenestra. Middle English had this word too, as fenester, but it lost against the Norse window.
